title: Why Your Student Loan Balance Keeps Growing

beats.say: You've been making your student loan payments for five years, so why is your total balance higher than the day you graduated?
beats.visual: A close-up of hands holding a plain blue pen over a dark wooden desk, dim moody lighting.

beats.say: How can your balance go up when you never missed a single payment?
beats.visual: A wide cinematic shot of a laptop glowing in a dark room, seen from behind the closed lid.

beats.say: Most people assume a monthly payment always chips away at the principal debt.
beats.visual: A low-angle shot of a classic desk lamp casting a warm circle of light on empty paper.

beats.say: That is false. On income-driven plans, your monthly check often only covers a fraction of the interest.
beats.visual: A macro shot of a metal paperclip resting on a stack of blank white sheets.

beats.say: So where does the rest of the monthly interest go?
beats.visual: A side profile of a coffee mug sitting on a dark kitchen counter at night.

beats.say: It doesn't vanish. It adds directly to your principal balance every single month.
beats.visual: A close-up of rain droplets sliding down a window pane with blurred city lights outside.

beats.say: Why does the system let unpaid interest stack up like that?
beats.visual: An overhead shot of an open leather notebook with no text inside, lit by soft window light.

beats.say: Because negative amortization is built into the math of low minimum payments.
beats.visual: A silhouette of a person standing by a large window looking out at a quiet street.

beats.say: Your balance balloons even though you pay on time.
beats.visual: A close-up of a wall calendar with blank squares, shot with a shallow depth of field.

beats.say: The rule is simple. If the payment doesn't beat the interest, the debt wins.
beats.visual: A dark hallway with a single bright lightbulb hanging from the ceiling.

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: A cinematic shot of a dark wooden staircase leading up into soft shadows.

caption: Your loan balance shouldn't grow when you're paying every month. Here is the math behind negative amortization. #personalfinance #money #studentloans #debt #financialliteracy
description: Discover why low income-driven student loan payments cause negative amortization and make your total balance grow every month.
first_comment: Did you know your payment could be lower than the monthly interest? Let us know in the comments.

facts.claim: Income-driven repayment plans can result in negative amortization where unpaid interest adds to the principal balance.
facts.basis: Standard federal student loan repayment rules for income-driven plans.

loop_map.stakes: Making student loan payments for five years while the total balance increases.
loop_map.big_question: Why is your total balance higher than the day you graduated?
loop_map.assume: Most people assume a monthly payment always chips away at the principal debt.
